papers.title: Weak-to-Strong Generalization via Direct On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) is a powerful recipe for improving language-model reasoning, but it is expensive to repeat on every new strong model because the target model must generate many rollouts during training. As models scale, post-training itself becomes a bottleneck. We study a weak-to-strong alternative: run RL on a smaller model where rollouts are cheaper, then reuse what that RL run learned to improve a stronger target model. Directly distilling the post-RL weak teacher is not enough, because the teacher's final policy mixes useful RL gains with the limitations of the smaller model. We propose Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD), which transfers the teacher's RL-induced policy shift instead. Direct-OPD compares the post-RL teacher with its own pre-RL reference and treats their log-ratio as a dense implicit reward for the student. In plain terms, the checkpoint pair tells us which actions RL made the weak model more or less likely to take, and Direct-OPD applies that signal on the stronger student's own on-policy states. This directly reuses the weak model's RL supervision signal without training an explicit reward model or running sparse-reward RL on the target model. Empirically, Direct-OPD consistently leverages weaker teachers to improve stronger target models; notably, it boosts Qwen3-1.7B from 48.3% to 62.4% on AIME 2024 in just 4 hours on 8 A100 GPUs. It outperforms step-matched direct RL and enables the sequential composition of multiple policy shifts. Our results show that RL outcomes can be reused across model scales as implicit reward signals, not merely as final models to imitate.

summary.takeaway: Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) transfers RL-induced policy shifts from smaller weak teachers to stronger target models, improving performance efficiently without explicit reward modeling or direct RL on large models.
summary.problem: Re-running reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) on every new large language model is computationally expensive and becomes a bottleneck as model scale increases.
summary.method: Direct-OPD computes the log-ratio between a weak teacher’s post-RL and pre-RL policies as an implicit dense reward, applying this signal on the stronger student’s own on-policy states to transfer RL improvements.
summary.evidence: Empirically, Direct-OPD boosts Qwen3-1.7B accuracy on AIME 2024 from 48.3% to 62.4% in 4 hours on 8 A100 GPUs, outperforming step-matched direct RL and generalizing across teacher-student pairs.
summary.limitations: Direct-OPD can fail when the teacher/reference improvement is not meaningful on student-visited states, and optimal response length and KL regularization strength depend on the teacher-student pair.
summary.why_for_you: This method offers a statistically principled approach to reuse RL outcomes across model scales via implicit reward signals, addressing computational bottlenecks in on-policy distillation for large language models.

signals.text: Direct-OPD leverages the policy-as-reward identity by using the log-ratio of post-RL and pre-RL weak teacher policies as a dense implicit reward, enabling transfer of RL-induced improvements without explicit reward models.

The method applies the implicit reward signal on the student’s own on-policy states, avoiding imitation of the weak teacher’s final policy which may limit stronger students due to the weak model’s capacity constraints.

Experiments show Direct-OPD improves students that already exceed the weak teacher’s performance, with consistent gains across different teacher pairs, student families, and training pipelines, demonstrating robustness and generalization.

deep_dive.overview: The paper addresses the computational inefficiency of applying reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) directly on large language models by proposing a weak-to-strong transfer paradigm called Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD). Instead of training RL on the large target model, RL is run on a smaller, cheaper weak model. Direct-OPD extracts the RL-induced policy shift by computing the log-ratio between the weak teacher’s post-RL and pre-RL policies, treating this as a dense implicit reward. This reward signal is then applied on the stronger student’s own on-policy states, enabling the student to learn the improvement direction without imitating the weak teacher’s final policy, which may be suboptimal. Empirical results on the AIME 2024 benchmark demonstrate that Direct-OPD significantly improves stronger models like Qwen3-1.7B, outperforming direct RL baselines with less compute. The approach generalizes across different teacher-student pairs and supports sequential composition of multiple policy shifts. This reframes RL outcomes as reusable improvement signals rather than final policies to imitate, offering a scalable solution for post-training large language models.

methodology.title: Policy Shift Computation
methodology.detail: Direct-OPD computes the log-ratio between the post-RL teacher policy and its own pre-RL reference policy, representing the RL-induced policy shift as a dense implicit reward signal.

methodology.title: On-Policy Distillation with Implicit Reward
methodology.detail: The student model samples its own on-policy states and is trained to maximize the implicit reward derived from the teacher’s policy shift, enabling transfer of RL improvements without explicit reward modeling.

methodology.title: Avoiding Imitation of Weak Teacher
methodology.detail: Unlike vanilla on-policy distillation that imitates the weak teacher’s final policy, Direct-OPD transfers only the policy shift, preventing degradation when the student already surpasses the teacher.

methodology.title: Training Setup and Hyperparameters
methodology.detail: Training uses a global batch size of 64, rollout length of 4, learning rate of 1e-6, and KL coefficients adapted per teacher-student pair; evaluation uses AIME 2024/2025 benchmarks with 32 samples per problem and temperature 0.7.

mechanism.title: Policy-as-Reward Identity
mechanism.detail: Under KL-regularized RL, the log-ratio of the policy to a reference recovers the reward up to a constant; Direct-OPD uses this identity in reverse to extract a dense implicit reward from the difference between post-RL and pre-RL teacher policies.

experiments.title: Weak-to-Strong Transfer Across Models
experiments.detail: Transferred policy shifts from R1-Distill-1.5B → JustRL-1.5B and Nemotron-1.5B → QuestA-Nemotron-1.5B teacher pairs into stronger students R1-Distill-7B, Qwen3-1.7B, and Qwen3-4B, evaluated on AIME 2024 and 2025 benchmarks.

experiments.title: Comparison with Direct RL
experiments.detail: Direct-OPD outperforms step-matched direct RL baselines in accuracy and compute efficiency, boosting Qwen3-1.7B from 48.3% to 62.4% accuracy on AIME 2024 in 4 hours on 8 A100 GPUs.

experiments.title: Sequential Composition of Policy Shifts
experiments.detail: Demonstrated that multiple independently learned policy shifts can be composed sequentially to accumulate gains in a single student model.

findings.title: Improvement Beyond Teacher Performance
findings.detail: Direct-OPD improves students whose initial accuracy already exceeds the post-RL weak teacher, indicating that transferring the policy shift is more effective than imitating the teacher’s final policy.

findings.title: Generalization Across Teacher-Student Pairs
findings.detail: The method generalizes across different teacher families, training pipelines, and datasets, as shown by consistent improvements transferring from both JustRL and QuestA teacher pairs.

findings.title: Compute Efficiency
findings.detail: Direct-OPD achieves significant accuracy gains with substantially less compute than running RL directly on the large target model, addressing the post-training bottleneck.

findings.title: Robustness to Prompt and Dataset Variations
findings.detail: Similar transfer trends are observed when changing prompt templates and training datasets, indicating robustness of the approach.

contributions: Proposed Direct On-Policy Distillation (Direct-OPD) to transfer RL-induced policy shifts from weak to strong models.
Demonstrated that the policy shift log-ratio serves as a dense implicit reward for efficient knowledge transfer.
Showed empirical improvements on large language models across multiple teacher-student pairs and benchmarks.
Established that RL outcomes can be reused as improvement signals rather than final policies to imitate.
Enabled sequential composition of multiple policy shifts to accumulate gains.
limitations: Direct-OPD can fail if the teacher/reference policy improvement is not meaningful on the student’s on-policy states.
Optimal response length and KL regularization strength are dependent on the specific teacher-student pair and require tuning.
The approach assumes availability of paired pre-RL and post-RL checkpoints from the weak teacher.
No explicit mechanism is provided for handling cases where the weak teacher’s policy shift is noisy or misaligned.
open_questions: How to automatically adapt KL regularization and response length parameters for arbitrary teacher-student pairs?
Can Direct-OPD be extended to transfer policy shifts from multiple weak teachers simultaneously?
What are the theoretical limits of policy shift transfer when student and teacher architectures differ substantially?
How does Direct-OPD perform on tasks with sparse or delayed rewards beyond reasoning benchmarks like AIME?
